reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Manage as a trauma patient using the primary survey, with haemorrhage control as the priority once the airway is secure
A haemodynamically unstable patient or one with peritonitis or evisceration needs immediate surgery rather than further imaging
Gunshot wounds usually breach the peritoneum and injure viscera and generally warrant laparotomy, whereas selected stab wounds may be managed non-operatively with close observation
Do not remove an impaling object in the emergency setting; stabilise it and remove it in a controlled operative environment
The trajectory can be deceptive, so consider injury to the chest, retroperitoneum, and pelvis and inspect the back and flanks for other wounds
Serial abdominal examination detects evolving peritonitis in patients selected for conservative management
Give tetanus prophylaxis and early antibiotics when hollow-viscus injury is likely, and resuscitate with blood products in shock
reference.pathophysiology: A penetrating object breaches the abdominal wall and can lacerate solid organs (liver, spleen), causing haemorrhage, or hollow viscera (bowel, stomach), causing spillage of contents and peritoneal contamination. Vascular injury may produce rapid exsanguination into the peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneum. Low-energy stab wounds injure tissue along a relatively predictable track, whereas high-energy gunshot wounds transfer energy widely, causing cavitation and injury beyond the visible path. The result is a combination of haemorrhagic shock from bleeding and, later, peritonitis and sepsis from contamination.
additionalDifferentials: Superficial wound that has not breached the peritoneum
Associated thoracic injury from a thoraco-abdominal track
additionalInvestigations: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) to detect free intraperitoneal fluid
CT abdomen and pelvis in the stable patient to define trajectory and organ injury
Local wound exploration in selected stab wounds to assess peritoneal breach
Group and crossmatch with coagulation studies
Erect chest radiograph to detect free air or associated thoracic injury
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability indicating major haemorrhage and the need for immediate laparotomy
Peritonitis, evisceration, or a retained impaling object mandating surgical exploration
Gunshot trajectory crossing the peritoneal cavity
Rising lactate or persistent shock despite resuscitation
Evolving peritoneal signs during observation of a non-operatively managed wound
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the organs injured, blood loss, and time to control of haemorrhage and contamination. Early surgery for unstable or peritonitic patients improves survival, whereas delay allows exsanguination or sepsis with high mortality.
pitfalls: Removing an impaling object in the emergency department, which can trigger uncontrolled bleeding
Being reassured by a benign initial abdomen when injury can evolve
Underestimating trajectory and missing thoracic, retroperitoneal, or back wounds
Delaying surgery in an unstable patient to obtain imaging
Neglecting antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis when hollow viscus injury is likely
management: Follow a structured trauma primary survey, securing the airway and prioritising haemorrhage control
Resuscitate with balanced blood-product transfusion and activate the massive transfusion protocol for haemorrhagic shock
Proceed to immediate laparotomy for haemodynamic instability, peritonitis or evisceration
Stabilise any impaling object in situ and remove it only in a controlled operative setting
Select stable stab-wound patients for non-operative management with serial abdominal examination
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis given the risk of hollow-viscus contamination
Search for occult thoracic, retroperitoneal and pelvic injury and inspect the back and flanks for other wounds
Provide damage-control surgery and critical-care support for the unstable, coagulopathic patient
